solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Time in volcanic dust, mum wheezing

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside that other

blocks.note: ash is the dust a volcano throws out
T is the standard abbreviation for time
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: Someone caught in a cloud of volcanic ash while their mother struggles to breathe.
explanation.walkthrough: The time abbreviation sits inside the dust, so it splits that word in two before the informal word for mother is added on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition is a chronic lung complaint whose chief symptom is laboured, whistling breathing, so the noun sense of wheezing stands for it.

clue.text: Type old Marple reformed

indicators.note: something reformed has been made over into a new shape, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: ex- means former, as in ex-husband
the name supplies its letters for rearranging

explanation.surface: A classic Miss Marple-style character has been given a makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: Marple suggests Agatha Christie's sleuth, but the name is just six letters to rearrange after EX.
explanation.definitionFit: A type in the sense of a perfect specimen or model is an exemplar, a typical or ideal instance of something.

clue.text: Little Kip put slimy mud under tin

indicators.note: in a down entry, being under something means coming after it in the order of letters

blocks.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
ooze is soft wet mud, as on a riverbed

explanation.surface: Someone called Little Kip is told to put sludge beneath a tin can.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital K makes Kip look like a name; kip is British slang for sleep. In a down clue, a piece placed under another follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Kip is informal British for a sleep, and a short, light sleep or nap is exactly a snooze.

clue.text: Gives up bitter to provide sudden impulse

blocks.note: to kick a habit is to give it up
tart means sharp or sour in taste

explanation.surface: Someone quits drinking bitter beer, hoping the change will give them a jolt.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British beer, which tempts you to think of drinking; here it is the adjective meaning sour.
explanation.definitionFit: To kick-start something is to give it a sharp initial push that sets it going, like a motorcycle engine.

clue.text: Someone with whom to pass time?

definitions.text: Someone with whom to pass time?

blocks.clueFragment: Someone with whom to pass time?
blocks.note: surface reading: a companion for whiling away the hours pleasantly
setter's reading: to pass time is to serve a sentence, so this is a fellow prisoner sharing your quarters

explanation.walkthrough: Passing time sounds like leisure with a friend; in prison slang, doing time means serving a sentence, and you do it alongside the person sharing your cell.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner's companion in confinement is literally the person with whom the sentence is served, side by side.

clue.text: Nothing in idle talk arises in brothel

indicators.note: in a down entry, something that rises is read from bottom to top, so its order is turned round

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written
gab is chatter, the gift of the gab

explanation.surface: Nothing in the gossip comes up in connection with a house of ill repute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but here it is taken literally as two letters in the string, which is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Bagnio is an old word, from Italian for a bathhouse, for a house of prostitution.

clue.text: Sweet animated penguin beheaded in pool

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter is cut off
something in another thing is placed inside it

blocks.note: a mere is a small lake or pool
Pingu is the claymation penguin of the children's TV series, minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A cute cartoon penguin meets a grisly end in a pool.
explanation.walkthrough: Pingu is a Swiss stop-motion children's show about a penguin; beheading drops its P.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet in the British sense of a dessert or confection: whipped egg white and sugar baked crisp.

clue.text: See 30
Travel to assess passing international point

indicators.note: to pass something is to go beyond it, so one part comes after the other

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for international
a tine is a prong or point, as on a fork or antler
to rate is to assess or value

explanation.surface: A traveller judging how to get across a border crossing point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' tells you the assessing word goes beyond the others, so it is written last.
explanation.definitionFit: To itinerate is to journey from place to place, especially on a circuit as a preacher or judge would.

clue.text: Bit for you in Paris coming up

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means reading upwards, so the order is turned round

blocks.note: French à toi, for you or yours

explanation.surface: A little something for you is on its way to Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' tells you to translate into French: à toi, written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An iota, the smallest Greek letter, is used to mean a tiny amount, as in not one iota.

clue.text: Edge forward in preparation to kill?

blocks.note: a hem is the edge of a piece of cloth
a lock is a forward in the rugby scrum

explanation.surface: A player inching forward as he gets ready to make the kill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edge forward' reads as a phrasal verb, to creep ahead, but splits into two nouns. In rugby, the lock is a second-row forward.
explanation.definitionFit: The poisonous plant was made into a deadly drink, famously the one Socrates was given, so it is a lethal preparation.

clue.text: Wobbly content of bulging loincloth

indicators.note: the content of something is what is inside it, so the outer letters are dropped
something wobbly is unsteady and shaken out of order

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An overstuffed loincloth whose contents are wobbling about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulging' and 'loincloth' both seem to be part of one comic picture, but only the inside of bulging is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A lungi is a cloth wrapped round the hips and legs, worn by men in South Asia, a kind of loincloth or sarong.

clue.text: Crowd on move in Foyle’s War maybe

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the following words, running across their boundaries

blocks.note: the run of letters straddles the three words

explanation.surface: A crowd scene in an episode of the wartime detective drama Foyle's War.
explanation.walkthrough: Foyle's War is a British TV detective series set in WWII; the answer runs from its apostrophe-s into maybe.
explanation.definitionFit: A swarm is a large crowd of people or insects moving together in a mass.

clue.text: First-class lieutenant keeping soldiers in disorder

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one part holds another inside

blocks.note: A1 means first-class, with the 1 written as I
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant
men are the ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A fine officer manages to keep his troops together in a chaotic rout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In disorder' looks like an anagram signal, but disorder is the definition in its medical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An ailment is an illness, and disorder in the medical sense means a disturbance of bodily or mental health.

clue.text: Surrounded by characters in team on grass

indicators.note: the letters are taken from inside the following words

blocks.note: the run of letters straddles the three words

explanation.surface: A player is mobbed by the rest of the team out on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like it means people, but here it means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the midst of a group is to be enclosed by its members, so the preposition matches.

clue.text: Without support, Walpole regularly beset by anxiety

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept
to be beset is to be surrounded on all sides

blocks.note: stress is mental strain or anxiety
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Prime Minister Walpole, abandoned by his allies, is racked with worry.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Walpole was Britain's first Prime Minister, so 'without support' reads as political; it is the definition of a dress or bra.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment without shoulder straps has none of the usual holding up, so it lacks that support.

clue.text: 30 8 20 male with Bounty cut down in capture

indicators.note: one thing placed in another goes inside it

blocks.note: he is the male pronoun
a bounty is a reward offered
to take is to capture
to hew is to chop or fell

explanation.surface: A man with a chocolate bar that has been chopped up during an arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 30 8 20 is ANGLO-SAXON NOBLE. Bounty is also a British chocolate bar, which suits a picture of something being cut down.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereward was an eleventh-century English thane who led resistance to the Norman conquest from the Fens, so he is a noble of that people.

clue.text: Chicken and vegetable for Casterbridge citizen

blocks.note: a hen is a female chicken
chard is a leafy green vegetable

explanation.surface: Someone in a country town ordering a chicken and greens dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Casterbridge is Thomas Hardy's fictional version of Dorchester.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Henchard is the title character of Hardy's novel The Mayor of Casterbridge, the town's leading inhabitant.

clue.text: Debris from clubs in crazy rag week

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it
something crazy is wild and disordered

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
the phrase supplies its letters for rearranging

explanation.surface: The mess left behind at nightclubs after a wild student charity week.
explanation.walkthrough: Rag week is a British university tradition of charity stunts; clubs looks like nightclubs but is the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris is scattered remains of something broken, which is what wreckage means.

clue.text: Lively Margate entertains one Xanadu poet

indicators.note: something lively moves about energetically, so the letters are stirred up
to entertain a guest is to have them inside your home

blocks.note: the place name supplies its letters for rearranging
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: The seaside resort of Margate plays host to a visiting poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Margate is a seaside town in Kent. Xanadu points to Coleridge, but the poet meant is the modern one who wrote a film-poem of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Armitage, UK Poet Laureate, wrote Xanadu, a poem-film set on a Rochdale housing estate.

clue.text: Head seen with pound, English coin

blocks.note: nob is slang for the head
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A monarch's head appears alongside the pound on an English coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English coin' reads as one phrase, but English gives only its letter and coin alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The noble was a medieval gold coin minted in England, worth a third of a pound.

clue.text: Check line penned by woman new to Union?

indicators.note: something penned is shut in an enclosure, so one part sits inside another

blocks.note: a bride is a woman just entering a marriage
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A newly joined member of a trade union writes a check line on a form.
explanation.walkthrough: Union with a capital looks like a trade union; it means marriage, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To bridle is to restrain or curb, as the headgear on a horse checks its movement.

clue.text: Goddess: smartie pants?

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish or poor, so the letters are in a bad state

blocks.note: the word supplies its letters for rearranging

explanation.surface: A clever goddess dressed in nothing but her underwear, like a cheeky caption.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants looks like trousers or underwear; in British slang it means rubbish, a signal to rearrange. Smarties are also a British sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: Artemis is the Greek goddess of the hunt and the moon, twin sister of Apollo.

clue.text: Temperature of old Peruvian container

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature
the Incas ruled ancient Peru

explanation.surface: Measuring the heat of an ancient Peruvian vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The split falls differently from the enumeration: T + INCAN reads as TIN CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin can is a sealed metal receptacle for food or drink, one kind of container.

clue.text: Dry and rocky peak in area

blocks.note: sec is the French term for dry wine
a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A description of a barren region with a craggy summit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' tempts as an anagram signal, but rocky peak together is a tor, a hill topped with rock in the southwest of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A sector is a distinct part or zone, of a city or a battlefield, which is an area.

clue.text: Romeo gripped by theatrical muscle pain

indicators.note: something gripped is held tight inside another's grasp

blocks.note: camp means exaggerated and theatrical
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An actor playing Romeo clutching himself in pain on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo and theatrical together suggest Shakespeare, but Romeo is just the radio code word for R.
explanation.definitionFit: A cramp is a sudden painful involuntary contraction of a muscle.

clue.text: Bark associated with golden retriever?

blocks.note: surface reading: the sound a golden retriever dog makes
setter's reading: a bark is a sailing ship, and this one carried the hero who fetched back the Golden Fleece

explanation.walkthrough: A bark (or barque) is a sailing vessel. Jason sailed to Colchis with his crew to retrieve the Golden Fleece, so the golden retriever is him, not a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this was the ship of Jason and his Argonauts on the quest for the Fleece.

clue.text: Rustic devouring duck in lift

indicators.note: to devour is to swallow, so one part ends up inside another

blocks.note: a hick is an unsophisticated country person
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, written O

explanation.surface: A country bumpkin eating a duck while riding in an elevator.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a duck is a batsman's score of zero, so it gives O.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoick is informal British for hauling or yanking something upward abruptly.

clue.text: Nuts, plum and date nice where all discovered?

indicators.note: to discover is to remove the cover, so each word loses its outside letters

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A shopping list of nuts, plums and dates, all nicely uncovered.
explanation.walkthrough: Nuts sits in a list of fruit, but it is the definition in its slang sense of crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts is slang for mad, and lunatic as an adjective means wildly foolish or insane.

clue.text: Scrupulous one bound by monastic vows

blocks.note: first meaning: painstakingly regular and conscientious
second meaning: as a noun, a monk or nun

explanation.surface: A conscientious person who has taken holy orders.
explanation.walkthrough: The adjective and the noun are spelt the same; a religious is a member of a monastic order.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both meticulously faithful in habit and, as a noun, a person living under monastic vows.

clue.text: Slogan abused American feller using blunt language

indicators.note: something abused is mistreated and knocked out of shape

blocks.note: the word supplies its letters for rearranging
ax is the American spelling of axe, a tool for felling trees
on as in on drugs, taking or using

explanation.surface: An American bloke shouting a slogan full of swear words.
explanation.walkthrough: Feller looks like 'fellow', but it means something that fells. On means using, as in being on medication.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglo-Saxon is used for plain, coarse English vocabulary, the short swear words that derive from Old English.
